Fig. 76 Lynda Roberts, Vox Populi: Climate for Opinion; 
2010, live narrow cast radio station with speaker 
installation. Courtesy of Arsineh Houspian. 
Reproduced with permission by the artist. 
Fig. 77 Qinglan Huang, Circus, 2010, interactive sculptural 
installation. Courtesy of Arsineh Houspian. 
Reproduced with permission by the artist. 
Fig. 78 Sarah Duyshart and Jen Rae, In Medias Res, 2010, 
parallel interactive installations using smoke and 
snow, documentation photographs. Courtesy of 
Arsineh Houspian. Reproduced with permission by 
the artists. 
Fig. 79 Mountain pine beetle, 2010, photograph. Courtesy 
of Critter Get Ritter. Retrieved 8 November 2014 
from Critter Get Ritter, 
<http://crittergetritter.com/mountain-pine-beetle>. 
Fig. 80 Blue stain fungi – approximately 1 cm, West Don 
Valley, 2010. Courtesy of Toronto Wildlife. 
Retrieved from Toronto Wildlife on 8 November 
2014, <http://toronto-
wildlife.com/Fungi/Mushrooms/ascomycota/more_
blue_stain.html>. 
Fig. 81 Pine beetle infested forest, 2007, photograph. 
Reproduced with permission courtesy of Simon 
Fraser University and Dezene Huber. Retrieved 
from Flickr, <https://flic.kr/p/e8SuXx>. 
Fig. 82 Dead forest from pine beetle infestation in Alberta, 
Canada, 2012, photograph.  
Fig. 83 In Medias Res (snow/Canada), 2010, Melbourne 
City Square, interactive sculptural installation: 
acrylic paint, artificial snow, clay, flocking, glue, 
ground snow (super absorbent polymer) and snow 
blowing machine. 
Fig. 84 Public interaction with In Medias Res 
(snow/Canada), 2010, Melbourne City Square. 
Courtesy of Arsineh Houspian and Jen Rae. 
Fig. 85 Exponential growth/Exponential decay, 2010, digital 
photograph. 
Fig. 86 Exponential growth/Exponential decay, 2010, 
proposed public art installation for the City of 
Melbourne CH2 building. 
Fig. 87 Joseph Beuys, 7,000 Oak Trees/ 7,000 Eichen, 1982, 
photograph. On 16 March 1982, Beuys planted the 
first tree of his Documenta 7 artwork in front of the 
Museum Fridericianum. Courtesy of Joseph Beuys. 
Retrieved 26 January 2015 from Kassel, 
<http://www.kassel.de/kultur/documenta/kunstwer
ke/objekte/08259>. 
Fig. 88 Grazing livestock, 2015, photograph, Puhi Puhi, 
New Zealand. 
Fig. 89 Still livestock, 2014, digital photograph.  
Fig. 90 Riparian land cross-section depicting best practice 
in riparian land management in contrast to the 
damage caused by unrestricted livestock grazing, 
2010, illustration. Courtesy of Jen Rae and The 
Riparian Project. 
Fig. 91 Riparian zone damage caused by heavy hooved 
animals accessing the Ingegoodbee River, Victoria, 
2014. Courtesy of Alexandra Blucher. Retrieved 17 
January 2015 from ABC, 
<http://www.abc.net.au/news/2014-02-27/stream-
bank-damage-in-kosciuszko/5282994>. 
Fig. 92 Cow eliminating in the Barham River, near Apollo 
Bay, Victoria, 2014, photograph. Courtesy of Sally 
Beattie. 
Fig. 93 Peter Solness, Grazing Line, Macquarie Marshes, 
NSW, 2002, photograph. Reproduced with 
permission courtesy of the photographer. 
Fig. 94 Henry Gritten, Melbourne from the Southbank of the 
Yarra River, 1856, watercolour over traces of pencil, 
25.6cm x 35.8cm. Reproduced with permission from 
the National Gallery of Victoria, Melbourne. Gift of 
John H. Connell, 1914. Retrieved 17 January 2015 
from the National Gallery of Victoria, 
<http://www.ngv.vic.gov.au/col/work/27227>. 
Fig. 95 Unrestricted livestock grazing in the Glenelg River, 
Victoria., 2009. This is one of the top flow stressed 
rivers in the state and has numerous crown 
frontages. The water you see is the most that this 
river has had in the last 7 years. It has been mostly 
dry for over this period of time. Courtesy of 
Amanda Wealands and The Riparian Project. 
Fig. 96 Photograph in the 2014 Devondale calendar 
showing unrestricted livestock in a riparian zone. 
Courtesy of Devondale. 
Fig. 97 The Riparian Project team members left to right: Jen 
Rae, Nicola Rivers and Amanda Wealands, 2009, 
Yea Wetlands, Victoria. 
Fig. 98 The Riparian Project team receiving the RMIT 
SEEDS grant. Here with Mary Crooks (L) and Liz 
McAloon from The Victorian Womens Trust/Our 
Watermark. 
Fig. 99 Map showing the distance between Yea and 
Melbourne, Victoria. Courtesy of Google Maps.  
Fig. 100 A crowd lining the Yea River on Carnival Day, circa. 
1905. Courtesy of The Biggest Family Album of 
Australia, Museum Victoria. Retrieved 16 January 
2015 from Museum Victoria, 
<http://museumvictoria.com.au/collections/items/7
70337/negative-yea-victoria-circa-1905>. 
Fig. 101 Amanda discussing the aims and objectives of The 
Riparian Project to Yea community members at a 
fundraising dinner for the Y Water Discovery 
Centre, 2011, photograph. Courtesy of The Riparian 
Project.  
Fig. 102 The first gathering of the Public Art Advisory 
Group, which included a facilitated tour of the Yea 
Wetlands and workshop on public art, July 2011, 
photographs. Courtesy of The Riparian Project. 
Fig. 103 Yue Minjun, A-maze-ing Laughter, 2009, 14 
patinated bronze figures each 3 metres tall, 
Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada. Courtesy of 
the artist. Retrieved 1 February 2015 from Blue Nose
